A:
**A chunk is an evidence retrieval unit, not an arbitrary slice of characters.** Start with document structure: headings, paragraphs, tables, lists and exception clauses. Preserve enough surrounding meaning to interpret the passage, while keeping chunks small enough for selective retrieval. Tokenize with the target model when enforcing hard model limits; a word-count estimate is only a planning aid. Retain the original source span and transformation profile so copied text can be audited.

A fixed-window splitter is predictable but can separate 'returns within 30 days' from 'except final-sale items'. Overlap improves boundary recall at the cost of duplicate candidates, storage and context tokens. Heading-aware splitting keeps sections intact but may produce oversized tables. A parent/child strategy retrieves small children and resolves a permitted parent; recheck access and budgets at expansion. Do not expand a visible paragraph into a confidential parent section.

**Work the evidence budget.** If the model permits 4,096 tokens, reserve 512 output, 384 system/tool instructions and 256 conversation tokens: 2,944 remain for retrieved evidence and separators. This is arithmetic under stated assumptions, not a provider capability claim. Packing five 700-token passages does not fit. Select evidence for marginal claim coverage, remove repeated overlap, and retain both the general rule and decisive exception. Prefer abstention to silently dropping the clause that changes the answer.

Evaluate chunking jointly with retrieval and citation quality. Compare fixed, structural and overlapping policies on the same revision-specific gold spans; record candidate recall, duplicate rate, final-context coverage and total tokens. A bigger chunk can improve recall while lowering precision or hiding the exception in a long context. The policy capstone uses lossless sentence chunks to expose spans and a deliberately removed exception; it does not assert that sentence chunking wins on scanned tables or multilingual documents. Revisit splitting when the parser, embedding model or source layout changes.
Why: The general return rule and final-sale exception are separate spans. A top-k answer that includes only the general rule can be wrong even with a valid citation; the assessment must require decisive exception coverage.
Risk: Overlap can make one fact appear repeatedly and dominate ranking, while stripping headings can erase conditions needed to interpret a table or list.
Trade: Small chunks improve targeting but require context reconstruction. Large chunks reduce fragmentation while increasing irrelevant tokens and privacy exposure to downstream models.
Try: Compute the 2,944-token evidence allowance independently. Design three chunk boundaries for a rule plus exception, then identify which policy preserves source spans and decisive evidence under a smaller budget.

follow_ups.Q: What changes for a table split across scanned pages?
follow_ups.A: Preserve row/column headers, page coordinates and continuation relationships. OCR and layout reconstruction become part of the versioned transformation; a text-only sentence splitter is insufficient, so evaluate labeled table questions separately.

Q: Does a sliding-window chunker count tokens, words, or characters?
Why: Token-accurate chunking guarantees that chunks will never exceed the context window of downstream embedding models and prevents silent truncation of vital text at the tail of chunks.
Risk: Counting characters instead of tokens causes code blocks and non-English text to overflow embedding model limits, resulting in silent loss of all text past the model's max token cutoff.
Trade: Tokenizing text during chunking consumes slightly more CPU than naive string slicing, but guarantees 100% compliance with embedding and LLM context limits.
Try: Tokenize 500 characters of English text versus 500 characters of Python code using tiktoken. Compare the token counts to observe how character-based chunking produces drastically uneven token lengths.

Q: How does overlap affect recall and ingestion cost?
Why: Balancing overlap preserves complete semantic thoughts across boundaries while keeping vector database storage and embedding generation budgets strictly under control.
Risk: Zero overlap causes critical policy conditions or table rows to be split across chunks, resulting in retrieval failures and misinformed model answers.
Trade: A 10–15% overlap provides sufficient context continuity while adding only modest 10–15% storage overhead compared to aggressive 50% overlap.
Try: Chunk a 5,000-token document using chunk_size=500 with overlap=0 versus overlap=100. Count total chunks, calculate storage inflation, and verify that sentences spanning boundaries remain intact in the overlapping version.

Q: Why validate that overlap is smaller than chunk_size?
Why: Defensive parameter validation prevents infinite loops and catastrophic pipeline hangs during automated batch document ingestion.
Risk: Allowing unvalidated configuration to set overlap >= chunk_size freezes backend ingestion workers in infinite CPU loops, blocking the entire document ingestion queue.
Trade: Adding startup assertion checks takes 2 lines of code and eliminates a class of critical pipeline freeze bugs.
Try: Write a unit test for a chunker constructor verifying that initializing Chunker(chunk_size=500, overlap=500) immediately raises a ValueError("overlap must be strictly less than chunk_size").

Q: How does a section-aware chunker preserve semantic structure?
A:
A section-aware (structural / semantic) chunker splits documents along natural document hierarchies (Markdown headers, HTML sections, JSON keys, or paragraph breaks) rather than blindly chopping at arbitrary token counts:

Recursive Splitting Hierarchy: (1) Level 1 (Major Headings): Split on top-level section dividers ("
# ", "
## "); (2) Level 2 (Paragraphs): Split on double newlines ("

"); (3) Level 3 (Sentences): Split on sentence terminators (". ", "? ", "! "); (4) Level 4 (Words & Characters): Split on spaces (" ") only when a single sentence exceeds the maximum chunk size;

Context Inheritance: A sophisticated section-aware chunker prepends the parent section hierarchy (e.g., "[Policy > Section 4: Refunds]\n") to the beginning of every child chunk. This ensures that even if a sub-chunk contains only a bulleted list of dates, its embedding vector retains the semantic context of the parent policy topic, drastically improving retrieval accuracy.
Why: Respecting natural document boundaries and prepending section headings ensures that chunks are self-contained semantic units that can be understood by both the embedding model and the downstream LLM.
Risk: Naive fixed-length character chunking cuts sentences and code blocks in half, producing disjointed fragments that ruin embedding coherence and hallucinate context.
Trade: Section-aware chunking requires parsing document structure (Markdown/AST), but produces vastly higher retrieval precision than brute-force slicing.

Q: Are chunk IDs deterministic in this implementation?
A:
In production RAG systems, chunk IDs must be DETERMINISTIC and REPRODUCIBLE, not random UUIDs generated on the fly:

Deterministic ID Generation Pattern: chunk_id = sha256(f"{document_id}:{chunk_index}:{content_hash}").hexdigest()

Why Deterministic IDs are Mandatory: (1) Idempotent Ingestion & Deduplication: If an ingestion job fails halfway through a 1,000-page document and is retried, deterministic IDs allow the database to execute an idempotent upsert (ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE). The database overwrites or skips identical chunks without creating duplicate records; (2) Cache Invalidation & Lineage Tracking: When updating or re-indexing a document, the system can compute new chunk IDs and immediately identify which chunks were modified, which are new, and which obsolete chunks should be deleted; (3) Deterministic Trace Citations: Allows audit logs and frontend citations to refer to immutable, reproducible chunk references across re-runs.
Why: Deterministic content-hashed chunk IDs make document re-ingestion idempotent, preventing duplicate chunks and enabling precise cache invalidation.
Risk: Using random UUIDs on every ingestion run creates thousands of duplicate vector records when pipelines retry after network drops, bloating database storage and polluting search results.
Trade: Computing SHA-256 hashes adds negligible CPU overhead (<1 microsecond per chunk), but provides rock-solid idempotency and auditability.
Try: Implement a chunk_id generator using hashlib.sha256. Re-run it twice on the same document and verify that the exact same chunk IDs are generated both times.

Q: Why must chunker configuration be part of an ingestion fingerprint?
A:
An Ingestion Fingerprint is a cryptographic hash of all parameters and source artifacts governing document ingestion: fingerprint = sha256(f"{doc_content_hash}:{chunk_size}:{overlap}:{tokenizer_name}:{embed_model_id}").hexdigest()

Why It Must Be Recorded: (1) Semantic Compatibility: If an engineer alters chunk_size from 500 to 250, or changes overlap from 50 to 100, the existing chunks in the database represent a completely different semantic segmentation. If the ingestion pipeline does not track the chunker fingerprint, it cannot detect that the stored vectors are out-of-date and must be re-chunked; (2) Embedding Model Pairing: Embeddings are intimately paired with their chunk lengths. Changing chunking parameters without re-indexing invalidates retrieval calibration; (3) Automated Cache Invalidation: Storing the ingestion fingerprint in document metadata allows ingestion pipelines to check: if stored_fingerprint == current_fingerprint: skip_ingestion() (saving thousands of dollars in redundant embedding API calls).
Why: Recording ingestion fingerprints provides cryptographic provenance, automated cache invalidation, and guarantees that stored vectors match the current chunking and embedding configuration.
Risk: Changing chunk_size in code without fingerprint tracking leaves old, incompatible chunks in the vector database, causing degraded retrieval performance that goes undetected.
Trade: Storing fingerprints requires a metadata column in the documents table, but saves massive re-embedding compute costs by skipping unchanged files.
Try: Write a function that calculates an ingestion fingerprint. Modify chunk_size by 10% and verify that the fingerprint changes, triggering an automatic re-ingestion flag.

Q: What would parent-child or hierarchical retrieval add?
Why: Hierarchical retrieval combines the laser precision of small-chunk vector matching with the rich context of large-chunk LLM generation, substantially improving RAG answer quality.
Risk: Feeding only tiny 100-token chunks directly to an LLM produces incomplete, fragmented answers because surrounding qualifications and definitions were omitted.
Trade: Parent-child indexing requires storing parent text blobs and maintaining relational parent-child keys, but eliminates context fragmentation without hurting retrieval precision.
Try: Implement a parent-child chunker: split text into 1,000-token parents and 200-token children. Match on child vectors and verify that returning the parent text provides complete contextual explanations.

Q: How should chunking change for code, tables, and multilingual documents?
Why: Tailoring chunking logic to document modality preserves syntactical validity in code, columnar alignment in tables, and semantic integrity in multilingual texts.
Risk: Chopping tables without repeating column headers creates orphan data chunks that LLMs cannot interpret, leading to hallucinations in quantitative queries.
Trade: Format-specific parsing (tree-sitter for code, table extractors for HTML) adds preprocessing complexity, but is essential for specialized enterprise RAG.
Try: Take a 20-row Markdown table and chunk it using a naive text splitter versus a table-aware splitter that repeats the header row. Observe the difference in readability of the 2nd and 3rd chunks.

Q: How do I tune chunking scientifically?
A:
Tuning chunking parameters (chunk_size and overlap) should be conducted as an empirical, hypothesis-driven machine learning experiment, not by guessing arbitrary numbers:

Scientific Tuning Protocol: (1) Curate a Golden Evaluation Set: Assemble 50–100 representative query-answer pairs with annotated ground-truth source document spans; (2) Grid Search Experiment: Chunk the corpus across a discrete parameter grid: chunk_sizes = [128, 256, 512, 1024 tokens] x overlaps = [0%, 10%, 20%]; (3) Measure Retrieval Metrics: Compute Recall@k, HitRate@k, and NDCG@k for each grid configuration. Identify which chunk size maximizes recall without exceeding your context budget; (4) Measure Generation Quality: Run end-to-end RAG over the top-performing configurations and measure Faithfulness and Answer Relevance (using Ragas or DeepEval); (5) Cost & Latency Pareto Analysis: Select the configuration on the Pareto frontier that delivers acceptable recall at the lowest vector storage cost and retrieval latency.
Why: Empirical tuning grounds chunking decisions in quantitative benchmark data, ensuring that parameters are optimized for the specific domain corpus and user query distribution.
Risk: Arbitrarily choosing chunk_size=1000 because of internet tutorials can degrade retrieval recall by 40% if your domain queries are short, specific factual questions.
Trade: Running an empirical grid search requires annotating an evaluation dataset and running multi-hour benchmark sweeps, but guarantees optimal production retrieval performance.
Try: Set up an experiment script using 30 test questions: evaluate HitRate@5 for chunk_sizes 256, 512, and 1024, plotting the resulting recall curve against total chunk count.
